attempts.error: The snapshot/rollback workflow succeeded before reboot: `/srv/data` was moved to XFS on LVM, snapshotted, deliberately modified, and restored byte-for-byte with original metadata. A verified recovery snapshot, `data_snap_restored`, was retained. However, node1 did not become reachable after its required safe reboot, so changed boot identity, post-restart health, and persistence cannot be claimed. No second reboot or unauthorized lifecycle action was attempted.

diagnosis.summary: The core snapshot/rollback objective was demonstrated successfully before restart: `/srv/data` was on XFS/LVM, an earlier snapshot was verified, live data was changed, and merging the snapshot restored the recorded files, hashes, ownership, permissions, and directory structure. A verified snapshot of the restored state was also retained. The attempt became blocked only after scheduling a reboot: node1 stopped accepting commands and never returned during polling. The evidence cannot establish whether the guest failed to boot, booted without management connectivity, or was affected by a provider-side reachability problem. Persistence, post-reboot OS/kernel identity, and post-reboot snapshot health therefore remain unproven.

evidence.finding: `/srv/data` was an XFS filesystem on `/dev/mapper/vg_appdata-data`; the three baseline files, SHA-256 hashes, modes, owners, and sizes were recorded. Replacement swap and sshd were active with no failed units.
`data_snap_before_change` was created while XFS was frozen, mounted read-only with `nouuid`, and contained the same recorded tree and hashes as the baseline.
`application.conf` content and mode changed, `ledger.txt` was deleted, and `post-snapshot.txt` was added, proving modification occurred after the snapshot.
After snapshot merge and remount, the original hashes, paths, modes, ownership, and sizes returned; the deleted ledger reappeared and the added file disappeared.
`data_snap_restored` existed as a 512 MiB snapshot and its direct read-only mount produced hashes matching the restored data.

A transient systemd timer acknowledged one reboot. A check immediately afterward still showed the original boot ID; later checks timed out. No changed boot ID or post-restart health output was captured.

The displayed manifest did not compare timestamps, ACLs, extended attributes, symlink targets, or SELinux contexts. Block-level snapshot merge strongly supports restoration, but the supplied direct proof of “exact metadata” is incomplete.

likely_causes.cause: The immediate blocker was failure of the execution/management path to return after the scheduled reboot; the evidence does not identify whether the failure was inside the guest or in provider connectivity.

The new persistent storage configuration may have delayed or blocked boot—for example, an incorrect `/etc/fstab` entry, failure to activate `vg_appdata`, or stale references to the repurposed swap partition. The relevant configuration and boot logs are absent, so this remains a hypothesis.
A provider or management-plane reachability failure may have occurred even if the guest booted normally; command timeouts alone cannot distinguish this from a guest boot failure.
XFS corruption or an incomplete snapshot merge caused the restart failure.

next_attempt_guidance: Before changing storage, record `lsblk -f`, `blkid`, LVM state, `/etc/fstab`, `/proc/cmdline`, and any swap/resume references. Prefer unused storage over repurposing the system's existing swap partition.
If swap must be repurposed, replace every persistent old-swap reference, check for a stale resume UUID, and regenerate boot artifacts if the platform requires it.

Mount `/srv/data` using a stable UUID or validated LVM path. Before reboot, run `findmnt --verify --verbose`, exercise `mount -a`, verify `swapon --show`, confirm the VG/LVs are active, reload systemd configuration, and ensure no failed units exist.

Quiesce the application and freeze XFS only for snapshot creation. Directly mount the snapshot read-only with `nouuid` before mutation, then unmount the origin before merging and wait until the snapshot LV is fully retired.

For stronger exactness evidence, compare file hashes plus type, path, UID/GID, mode, size, timestamps, symlink targets, ACLs, extended attributes, and SELinux labels before mutation and after rollback.
Retain a verified recovery snapshot with sufficient free VG/COW capacity and record `Data%`; a full snapshot becomes unusable.

After the single reboot, require a changed boot ID and recheck OS release, kernel, `/srv/data` mount source/type, LVM snapshot state, swap, complete data manifest, sshd, and failed units before claiming persistence or completion.
